currentContext.business: The Company develops and executes urban and civic infrastructure projects on PPP, EPC and turnkey models for both government and private clients, having transitioned from a localised real estate developer into a diversified urban infrastructure enterprise. Its core is affordable housing built around slum rehabilitation and redevelopment of housing, executed mainly in the state of Gujarat, alongside civic urban infrastructure such as bus terminals, BRTS corridors, healthcare and medical education facilities and multi-level parking. It also develops industrial parks, logistics warehousing and worker dormitories, and manages the full rehabilitation cycle from community assessment and relocation through construction and allotment to eligible beneficiaries.

Affordable housing / slum rehabilitation: EWS/LIG affordable housing aligned to PMAY / Housing for All
Civic urban infrastructure: Medical college campus / healthcare and medical education facilities

currentContext.expansion: Nila Infrastructures' expansion is project-pipeline driven rather than plant-capex driven, and the annual report describes it as footprint and units under execution rather than as a rupee capex programme. In slum rehabilitation - where the Company holds a leadership position in Ahmedabad and wins work through competitive bidding by municipal corporations and urban development authorities - over 6,500 housing units are currently under development, with individual project timelines ranging between 24 to 36 months and compensation received through Transferable Development Rights (TDRs) and/or land parcel allocations. In redevelopment of aging government housing board colonies, secured through formal tendering, over 3,500 units are currently under execution, with additional saleable units and TDRs as key revenue streams and a large base of aging colonies across Ahmedabad and other urban centres described as a significant long-term opportunity. In civic transport infrastructure, GSRTC has awarded the development and operation of bus terminal facilities at Amreli and Modasa on a DBFOT basis: Amreli (awarded solely to Nila) comprises a 7,719 sq. m built-up terminal with 12 boarding/alighting bays and 6 idle bays plus about 12,800 sq. m of commercial facilities under 90-year lease rights, while Modasa (awarded to a consortium with Vyapti Infrabuild Pvt. Ltd. in which Nila's share is 34%) comprises a 6,279 sq. m terminal with 11 boarding/alighting bays and 7 idle bays plus about 39,000 sq. m of commercial facilities under 90-year lease rights; the terminals are to feature iconic architecture, integrated commercial zones and modern passenger amenities. In industrial infrastructure, the Company has delivered 5 worker dormitories, 4 logistics warehouses and 1 commercial complex in joint venture with Kataria Group in Gujarat, and holds future-ready sites at Becharaji and Mandal, close to auto clusters and global OEMs such as Suzuki and Honda and with access to the Kandla and Mundra ports, positioned to meet rising demand for industrial units, warehousing and worker housing. The disclosed geographical footprint spans Gujarat (Ahmedabad, Amreli, Rajkot, Modasa, Surat, Vadodara, Sitapur, Naviyani) and Rajasthan (Udaipur, Jodhpur, Barmer, Bhilwada), and includes 9,578 EPC housing units, 104 BRTS stations, a 1,100 vehicle-capacity multi-level car parking, 9 lakh sq. ft. of commercial space, 720 media utilities, 2,906 dormitory beds, 5 lakh sq. ft. of warehouse space, 80,000 sq. ft. of commercial space, 56 acres of industrial park, and in Rajasthan a medical college campus supporting 100 MBBS admissions annually alongside housing blocks of 2,288, 1,152, 848 and 841 units. Chairman-level intent for the year ahead is to expand the Company's presence while deepening impact, explore innovative development models, adopt advanced construction practices and strengthen collaborations with government and institutional partners; the Board declined a dividend for FY2025-26 explicitly to retain financial resources for project execution and future growth. No rupee capital-expenditure quantum, capacity addition figure or commissioning date is stated anywhere in the routed text.

risks.note: The MD&A states that the majority of the Company's Principals/clients are government bodies, and that 'any significant change in government policy in promoting Affordable Housing and/or Urban Infrastructure could pose a threat'. Revenue therefore depends on the continuity of public schemes (PMAY, Housing for All, urban development programmes) and on municipal/state budget allocations rather than on private demand.

risks.risk: Execution and approval-cycle risk on long-gestation projects
risks.note: Listed as 'Execution risk' in the MD&A risk table, dependent on labour availability, raw material prices, receipt of approvals and regulatory clearances, access to utilities, weather conditions and absence of contingencies such as litigation. The MD&A adds that the approval process and time for projects are generally uncertain, which may delay execution and thereby affect financials; slum-rehabilitation project cycles alone run 24 to 36 months.

risks.risk: Input cost inflation and raw material / labour supply
risks.note: The MD&A flags 'Input cost fluctuations' - significant changes in raw material costs can impact profitability - and notes that timely supply of cement, steel and bricks is essential to complete projects, with shortages of labour and raw material capable of delaying execution. Mitigation relies on a competitive supply chain and the possible inclusion of raw material cost indexes in contractor/supplier agreements, meaning unindexed fixed-price contracts carry the exposure.

risks.risk: Capital intensity, liquidity and interest rate exposure
risks.note: The MD&A states that infrastructure projects are capital intensive and the business requires long-term commitment of capital to meet the financial requirement of long-term projects. It separately lists 'Interest rate risk' (interest costs impacted by market rates) and 'Liquidity risk' (acceptable liquidity levels are required to achieve desired financial results). The MD&A also observes that elevated financing costs and tighter liquidity conditions posed challenges for project execution and funding.

risks.risk: Credit / counterparty payment risk from Principals
risks.note: Listed as 'Credit risk' - the Principal's ability to pay can have an impact on the financial result. Given that the client base is dominated by government bodies and municipal authorities, receivable cycles and payment timing sit outside the Company's control; mitigation is limited to approving only well-established institutions/corporates as counterparties and continuous monitoring of exposure per counterparty.

risks.risk: Availability of skilled and technical personnel, and labour disputes
risks.note: The MD&A names timely availability of skilled and technical personnel as one of the key challenges, and lists 'Labour disputes' as a risk in which industrial action impacts the Company's ability to meet Principal/client demands. The stated mitigation is an open and positive relationship with employees, sub-contractors and workers, with the Company claiming not a single instance of such a dispute so far.

risks.risk: Competitive bidding pressure and technology obsolescence
risks.note: Listed as 'Competitor risk' - competitors find ways to bid at dramatically lower cost, or bid to construct with better functioning / latest technologies. Because the Company secures work through competitive bidding processes run by municipal corporations and urban development authorities, aggressive bidding by rivals directly compresses win rates or margins.

risks.risk: Cyclicality and macroeconomic sensitivity of the infrastructure order cycle
risks.note: The MD&A states the Company operates in a business which is cyclic in nature and that infrastructure projects are mainly dependent on economic scenarios, with any adverse events affecting the whole economy capable of deteriorating the industry. The separate 'Economic downturn' risk notes that the Company's customers could be impacted by a major economic downturn, resulting in lower demand for their respective projects.

risks.risk: Site-loss, climate and extreme weather disruption
risks.note: The MD&A flags 'Loss of a major project site' (fire, flood or natural disaster causing temporary loss of a construction operation plus reconstruction and remediation costs, putting time schedule, cost and revenues at risk) and 'Climate change risks - extreme weather events disrupt project execution', alongside supply chain disruption from fires, extreme weather, natural disasters, water stress, war or pandemic illness. Mitigation rests on insurance, loss-prevention programmes, emergency response plans including flood risk at all sites, and the diversification argument that the Company is operating on about 19 projects across Gujarat and Rajasthan so that if one project is taken out of action others could provide support - which also frames the underlying geographic concentration in just two states.
